'''James Charles Capers Jr.''' (born August 25, 1937) a [[United States Marine]] who received the [[United States]]'s highest military decoration, the [[Medal of Honor]], for heroism in Vietnam in March-April 1967.<ref>{{Cite web |title=James Capers Jr {{!}} Vietnam War {{!}} U.S. Marine Corps {{!}} Medal of Honor Recipient |url=https://www.cmohs.org/recipients/james-capers-jr |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Congressional Medal of Honor Society |language=en}}</ref>

==Early years==
Capers lived in [[Bishopville, South Carolina]], as a child but his sharecropper family left the [[Jim Crow era]] South for life in Baltimore, where he spent the rest of his youth and met his wife Dottie.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Capers Biography |url=https://www.capersthedoc.com/biography |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Major James Capers |language=en}}</ref>

==Medal of honor==
[[File:James Capers Jr., United States Marine Corps (cropped).jpg|thumb|James Capers Jr. (unknown date) ]]
In 2025, Congressman [[Ralph Norman]] introduced legislation to award Capers the Medal of Honor.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-06-19 |title=South Carolina Hero Major James Capers Jr. Awarded Medal of Honor |url=https://norman.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=3612 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=U.S. Representative Ralph Norman |language=en}}</ref> <ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-14 |title=Rep. Ralph Norman Reintroduces H.R. 3377 to Award the Medal of Honor to Major James Capers, Jr. |url=https://norman.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=2143 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=U.S. Representative Ralph Norman |language=en}}</ref> <ref>{{Cite web |last=Rep. Norman |first=Ralph [R-SC-5 |date=2026-03-26 |title=H.R.3377 - 119th Congress (2025-2026): To authorize the President to award the Medal of Honor to James Capers, Jr., for acts of valor as a member of the Marine Corps during the Vietnam War. |url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/3377 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> <ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-21 |title=Letter Sent to President Trump to Award Major James Capers, Jr. the Medal of Honor |url=https://norman.house.gov/news/documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=2047 |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=U.S. Representative Ralph Norman |language=en}}</ref> In 2026, US Senator [[Lindsey Graham]] introduced similar legislation, which was read and advanced.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Graham Celebrates Medal of Honor Awarded to South Carolina Veteran |url=https://www.lgraham.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/2026/6/graham-celebrates-medal-of-honor-awarded-to-south-carolina-veteran |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=United States Senator Lindsey Graham |language=en}}</ref>

On June 18, 2026, President [[Donald Trump]] awarded the Medal of Honor to Capers. Dignitaries present at the ceremony included [[Pete Hegseth]] and [[Gerald Malloy]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=House |first=The White |date=2026-06-18 |title=President Trump to Award Medal of Honor |url=https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2026/06/president-trump-to-award-medal-of-honor/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=The White House |language=en-US}}</ref> <ref>{{Cite web |last=Adams |first=Matthew |title=2 Marines and 1 soldier receive the Medal of Honor |url=https://www.stripes.com/history/2026-06-18/2-marines-1-soldier-medal-of-honor-22008436.html |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}}</ref> <ref>{{Cite news |last=Ismay |first=John |date=2026-06-18 |title=Three Medals of Honor Awarded to Vietnam and Afghanistan Veterans |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/18/us/politics/trump-medals-of-honor.html |access-date=2026-06-22 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The award came 60 years after Capers' actions in Vietnam.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Buchanan |first=Christopher |date=June 19, 2026 |title=Bleeding and severely wounded, a Marine from Bishopville saved his men. He was just awarded the Medal of Honor. |url=https://www.wltx.com/article/news/national/military-news/bishopville-marine-james-capers-medal-of-honor/101-f626039a-e714-4537-8045-de77fdf2ed8b |access-date=June 22, 2026 |work=WLTX-TV}}</ref>

==Medal of Honor citation==
{{blockquote|[[File:cmoh army.jpg|50px|center]]
The President of the United States of America, authorized by Act of Congress, March 3, 1863, has awarded in the name of Congress the Medal of Honor to
{{center|SECOND LIEUTENANT<br/>'''JAMES C. CAPERS JR.'''<br/>UNITED STATES MARINE CORPS}}

For conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty as a Team Leader with [[3d Force Reconnaissance Company]], 3d Reconnaissance Battalion in the [[South Vietnam|Republic of Vietnam]] from 31 March to 3 April 1967. Tasked to locate a [[People's Army of Vietnam|North Vietnamese]] regimental base camp southwest of [[Phú Lộc district|Phu Loc]] and provide observation for the flank of Company M, [[3rd Battalion, 26th Marines|3d Battalion, 26th Marines]], Second Lieutenant Capers maneuvered his nine-man team on a four-day patrol through rugged enemy territory. The team had contact with 20 enemy soldiers on the first day of patrol, and two additional contacts on the second day, resulting in one severely wounded team member. Despite being outnumbered by enemy forces, Second Lieutenant Capers relentlessly pursued his vigilant and tenacious adversary, and called for fire on an enemy base camp to thwart an impending attack on Company M. On the last day of the patrol, his team was engaged by a numerically superior enemy force with an initial attack from [[Claymore mine|claymore mines]], coupled with direct and indirect fire. Despite severe pain and blood loss caused by the multiple fragmentation and gunshot wounds he sustained, Second Lieutenant Capers bravely continued to lead his team and maintain the initiative. Even after being administered morphine, he continued to coordinate supporting fires and his team’s movement to a helicopter extraction site. While struggling to maintain consciousness and still under enemy attack, Second Lieutenant Capers maintained command of the situation to ensure all of his Marines were evacuated before he, barely able to stand, finally boarded the helicopter. By his bold leadership, undaunted courage, and complete dedication to duty, Second Lieutenant Capers reflected great credit upon himself and upheld the highest traditions of the Marine Corps and the United States Naval Service.}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cmohs.org/recipients/james-capers-jr|title=James Capers Jr|publisher=Congressional Medal of Honor Society|date=18 June 2026|access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref>

==Other recognition==
Capers was celebrated by Bishopville, South Carolina with the installation of three bronze plaques. One plaque is a map of North and South Vietnam. The other details Capers career. The middle plaque is a reproduction of a recruiting poster featuring Capers in his blue dress uniform with the words “Ask a Marine.” The three plaques are titled “The Place, The Legend, The Man.”<ref>{{Cite web |last=South |first=Todd |date=2020-10-09 |title=Black Force Recon Marine, battlefield commission, Vietnam War hero ... snubbed for the Medal of Honor? |url=https://www.marinecorpstimes.com/news/your-marine-corps/2020/10/08/black-force-recon-marine-battlefield-commission-vietnam-war-hero-snubbed-for-the-medal-of-honor/ |access-date=2026-06-22 |website=Marine Corps Times |language=en}}</ref> <ref>{{Cite news |title=The Place, The Legend, The Man |url=https://www.marines.mil/News/News-Display/Article/2337196/the-place-the-legend-the-man/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260126010048/https://www.marines.mil/News/News-Display/Article/2337196/the-place-the-legend-the-man/ |archive-date=2026-01-26 |access-date=2026-06-22 |work=United States Marine Corps Flagship |language=en-US}}</ref>:
